edition.deck: Conflict, economic pressure and contested decisions—from Ukraine and the US to Britain and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritised consequential developments and substantial reporting. Related coverage of the same event is grouped, with disputed claims and unresolved questions kept clear.

content.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties as northern fighting intensifies
content.shortHeadline:
Ethiopia and Eritrea
sever diplomatic ties
content.standfirst: The split comes as federal forces fight rebels in Ethiopia’s north, with the scale and causes of the renewed conflict still contested.

image.caption: Fighting has resumed in northern Ethiopia, where the UN warns civilians and aid operations are at risk.

sources.originalTitle: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates

segments.body: Ethiopia has closed its embassy in Eritrea and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave, accusing them of threatening national security. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic relations, saying it had no choice but to retaliate.

segments.title: Fighting and accusations
segments.body: Federal forces are battling the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and allied fighters across Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Both sides accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities; Ethiopia also accuses Eritrea of backing rebels, which Eritrea denies. The BBC says it has not independently verified an allegation that Eritrean soldiers are fighting in Tigray.

segments.title: Information remains limited
segments.body: Communications to Tigray are cut and the BBC says it cannot report from the region, making reliable information difficult to obtain. The UN says insecurity and road closures are disrupting aid and exposing civilians and infrastructure to danger.

content.headline: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September
content.shortHeadline:
US adds just 29,000 jobs
as unemployment edges up
content.standfirst: The weak report points to slower hiring, but economists caution that one month’s figures do not establish a lasting downturn.

image.caption: US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, according to official figures.

sources.originalTitle: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
USA's jobskabelse i september ligger langt under forventningerne

segments.body: US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, down from a revised 133,000 in August. Unemployment edged up from 4.1% to 4.2%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Hiring was little changed across major sectors, from technology to retail.

segments.title: A mixed economic signal
segments.body: Economists quoted by the BBC described the report as soft but not disastrous, and cautioned against drawing firm conclusions from volatile monthly figures. Danish economists cited by DR also disagreed on the broader picture: one called the figures disappointing and pointed to falling purchasing power, while another said other indicators still suggested continued US growth.

segments.title: Political and rate implications
segments.body: The report arrives a month before the US midterm elections and contrasts with President Donald Trump’s claims that the economy is booming. The BBC reports low approval ratings for his handling of the economy and cost of living. Economists said the data could reduce the likelihood of further Federal Reserve rate increases, though views on the outlook differ.

content.headline: Russian attacks intensify on Kyiv as winter fears grow
content.shortHeadline:
Russian strikes hit Kyiv
as winter fears grow
content.standfirst: Missile and drone attacks have damaged a school, hospital and bridge, while residents face outages and uncertainty over the city’s defences.

image.caption: A woman and child pass a site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
Russiske styrker angriber bro i Kyiv: 'Der er ikke nogen regler nu'

segments.body: Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, a school, a hospital and a major Kyiv bridge, according to reporting from the city. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said residents could no longer pretend life was continuing as in peacetime. Damage to the Pivdennyi Bridge has disrupted a key crossing over the Dnipro.

segments.title: Pressure on the capital
segments.body: The Guardian reports that some neighbourhoods have lost power and water after attacks on energy facilities. DR reports repeated hits on the Pivdennyi Bridge and says traffic on other crossings has also been affected. Ukraine’s president says Moscow has shifted its tactics; his account of an order to abandon the rules of war is based on intercepted communications and has not been independently verified by DR.

segments.title: Defences and the winter ahead
segments.body: Kyiv faces a shortage of Patriot interceptors and faster Russian drones that are harder to shoot down. Ukraine is developing interceptor drones, but sources told the Guardian it could take weeks or months to deploy them at scale. Ukrainian officials have warned European counterparts about a possible large-scale attack on energy infrastructure; the reported plan has not been independently confirmed in the material gathered.

content.headline: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives lethal injections
content.shortHeadline:
Tennessee pauses executions
after Pike survives injections
content.standfirst: Pike remains in hospital after two doses failed to kill her. Officials have ordered a review, but the state has not explained what went wrong.

image.caption: Christa Pike was receiving medical care after the attempted execution.

sources.originalTitle: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

segments.body: Christa Pike, 50, survived two injections of pentobarbital during an attempted execution in Tennessee. Her lawyers say she remained alive after the doses and was taken to hospital for life-saving care; her prognosis is unknown. Governor Bill Lee has halted executions in the state for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.

segments.title: What is known—and disputed
segments.body: Pike’s lawyers say staff struggled to establish an IV line and point to her blood-clotting condition and small veins. The state says it followed its established protocol, which does not specify further procedures after a second dose. Officials have not explained why the injections were non-fatal, and the department has not addressed the lawyers’ allegation that the drug may have been degraded.

segments.title: Calls for accountability
segments.body: Pike’s lawyers are seeking a commutation of her sentence. The Guardian reports calls from legal, medical and faith leaders for a wider halt to executions, citing concerns about repeated failures. The BBC’s account also includes veteran execution reporter Michael Graczyk’s view that the process must be witnessed and reported, alongside his concern that attention to Pike can eclipse her victim, Colleen Slemmer.

content.headline: French student protests spread as schools close and arrests mount
content.shortHeadline:
French student protests
spread across the country
content.standfirst: Students cite overcrowded classrooms, staff shortages and deteriorating buildings; the government condemns violence and police conduct is under scrutiny.

image.caption: Students blockade a high school in Paris as protests spread.

sources.originalTitle: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protests
The pictures that show the scale of France’s student protests

segments.body: Student protests over school conditions have spread across France. Police reported about 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents, with more than 160 schools shut; nearly 3,000 lycée students had been detained since the protests began, according to the interior ministry. Reports also describe fires and injuries.

segments.title: What students are demanding
segments.body: Pupils describe overcrowded classes, absent teachers, decaying buildings and classrooms that became unbearably hot during earlier heatwaves. The Guardian spoke to students who said they wanted decent conditions for learning. Reporting by the i Paper traces the movement’s spread from a school blockade in Créteil, amplified on TikTok, to demonstrations in cities around the country.

segments.title: A contested response
segments.body: The government has called the violence unacceptable and ordered security forces to reopen schools. Students and teachers have accused police of excessive force; the interior ministry has announced an internal investigation after allegations of brutality. Some teachers say they have joined blockades to protect pupils. The scale and conduct of the protests remain in flux.

content.headline: Cornell students demand answers over alleged 2024 gang rape
content.shortHeadline:
Cornell students demand
answers over rape case
content.standfirst: A civil lawsuit has revived allegations against seven students and Cornell. A criminal investigation has reopened; the men’s conduct and the university’s response remain contested.

image.caption: Cornell students speak at a public hearing about the case.

sources.originalTitle: 'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape
'Gratis fisse', skrev de i gruppechatten. Nu sagsøger kvindelig studerende syv mænd for gruppevoldtægt

segments.body: Students and faculty at Cornell University say anger and concern have spread across campus after an alleged gang rape from 2024 resurfaced. The accuser, identified as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house, and that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately discipline the men involved. The allegations have not been established in court.

segments.title: Investigations and university response
segments.body: New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state attorney general as special prosecutor after saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney. That office had previously concluded evidence did not meet the threshold for charges, then reopened its investigation after the civil complaint. Cornell says it conducted an extensive investigation and imposed sanctions, but says privacy law prevents it from disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes.

segments.title: Calls for transparency
segments.body: At a student assembly, students called for changes to assault policies and an external investigation. Cornell students quoted by the BBC described anger and a lack of transparency; DR’s report adds that the civil lawsuit says two men were expelled and others received suspensions, while Cornell disputes claims that the accused escaped meaningful discipline. More than 1,300 alumni have signed a letter calling for action.

content.headline: UN says gang violence has killed or injured more than 5,700 in Haiti
content.shortHeadline:
Haiti gang violence
leaves 5,700 dead or hurt
content.standfirst: The UN warns that gangs are expanding and recruiting more children, while questioning whether Haiti can hold credible elections in December.

image.caption: The UN says civilians have been caught in gang violence and security operations.

sources.originalTitle: More than 5,000 people killed or injured in Haiti due to gang violence this year, UN says

segments.body: More than 5,700 people were killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them in Haiti between 1 January and 11 September, the UN says. More than 230 people were kidnapped and an estimated 1,000 women and girls raped, a figure the UN says is likely higher.

segments.title: Violence and its consequences
segments.body: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk says gangs are seeking new territory and transport routes. More than half of the casualties occurred during security operations, with civilians also struck by stray bullets and explosive drones. The UN says recruitment of children into gangs has nearly tripled, as some minors see joining as their only means of survival.

segments.title: Election doubts
segments.body: Haiti is preparing for its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, scheduled for 13 December. Türk says it is hard to imagine the conditions for a credible vote being met this year. A multinational police force has been operating since 2025 but has struggled to enter areas controlled by gangs.

content.headline: Indian protesters demand election chief resign over voter-roll allegations
content.shortHeadline:
Indian protesters demand
election chief resign
content.standfirst: Thousands joined demonstrations over disputed voter-roll revisions. The Election Commission rejects accusations of rigging and says decisions were unanimous.

image.caption: India’s opposition parties have also called for the election chief to resign.

sources.originalTitle: India's 'cockroach' protesters are back - this time asking poll chief to resign

segments.body: Thousands of people rallied in Mumbai after the Cockroach Janta Party called for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign. The group says it will hold further demonstrations across India in October. Police detained hundreds of people attempting to protest in Delhi.

segments.title: Dispute over voter rolls
segments.body: The protests follow reporting that two other election commissioners had objected at least 14 times to decisions they said were made without their knowledge. The dispute centres in part on a revision of electoral rolls that has removed 130 million names. The Election Commission says the exercise removes duplicate and ineligible entries and that decisions were unanimous; opposition parties allege eligible voters have been removed to benefit the governing BJP. The claims are disputed.

segments.title: Calls for wider protests
segments.body: The Election Commission and Kumar have not responded to the latest calls for his resignation or the allegations of vote theft, and the BBC says it has sought comment. Opposition parties say they will hold rallies and plan a march to the Commission on 6 October.

content.headline: Government says diesel supply is secure as UK pump prices hit record
content.shortHeadline:
Ministers say diesel supply
is secure as prices soar
content.standfirst: The UK says it has varied sources and 42 days of reserves, while diesel prices have crossed £2 a litre and ministers discuss emergency stockpiles with European partners.

image.caption: The UK is discussing possible emergency diesel stock releases with European allies.

sources.originalTitle: Minister denies UK faces diesel shortage after Trump threatens to ban exports

segments.body: Transport minister Keir Mather says the UK is not facing a diesel shortage and that supplies come from a variety of sources. The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with most supplies coming from mainland Europe, and has reserves for 42 days, according to the Guardian.

segments.title: Prices and contingency planning
segments.body: The average UK diesel price reached a record 200.01p per litre on Friday, according to the RAC. The government has opened talks with European allies about releasing emergency stocks after the US threatened to cut off diesel exports unless allies released reserves. EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen said Europe was discussing the issue with all International Energy Agency members, not only the US.

segments.title: What remains uncertain
segments.body: The UK’s biggest refinery, Fawley, is due to close for up to 10 weeks of planned maintenance. The government says it is speaking to US officials and European partners; it has not announced a release of UK reserves. The fuel duty cut is extended until year-end, with its future to be set out at the budget.

content.headline: Burnham faces scrutiny after praising Manchester City owners
content.shortHeadline:
Burnham’s City praise
draws scrutiny
content.standfirst: The prime minister called Abu Dhabi’s owners a major partner in Manchester’s transformation as the club faces a continuing financial disciplinary process.

image.caption: Burnham speaking to a reporter after a match at the Etihad Stadium.

sources.originalTitle: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power
How Man City’s owners wooed Andy Burnham, from property deals to football chats

segments.body: Andy Burnham has drawn criticism after praising Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi United Group owners as a “huge partner” in building modern Manchester and saying he would be concerned if they left. The Premier League disciplinary process is continuing after the club was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules; City denies wrongdoing and plans to appeal.

segments.title: Investment and public land
segments.body: The Guardian examines the council’s Manchester Life partnership with the owners, which delivered private homes but no social or affordable housing. University of Sheffield researchers said the public land may have been leased too cheaply and described the deal as a transfer of public wealth to private hands. The council rejects that criticism, saying the land had no market interest at the time and the city benefits from investment and profit-sharing.

segments.title: The political response
segments.body: A Burnham ally called his comments a mistake, while No 10 said the independent process must run its course and anyone found to have done wrong should face consequences. Reporting also records arguments that City’s investment supported regeneration, jobs and facilities, alongside criticism over housing affordability and the owners’ wider influence.

content.headline: Police investigate whether two assaults near Aarhus are connected
content.shortHeadline:
Police probe two assaults
near Aarhus
content.standfirst: Investigators say it is too early to link the attacks. Police warn residents against forming private patrols and say extra officers will be visible in the area.

image.caption: Police say it is too early to tell whether the assaults are connected.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet efterforsker, om overfald på unge kvinder ved Risskov kan hænge sammen
Politi fraråder på det kraftigste ny patruljegruppe

segments.body: Police in East Jutland are investigating whether two assaults on women in Risskov, near Aarhus, are connected. A 22-year-old woman reported being knocked down, held and groped in July; a 24-year-old woman said she was pushed down and held in September before escaping. Police say it is too early to establish a link.

segments.title: Police advice
segments.body: Police say they have received further reports from women who felt unsafe, including one report of being followed, but have not established a connection to the assaults. They plan extra patrols and advise residents to continue their usual routines, travel with others if they feel unsafe, and report suspicious activity.

segments.title: Warning against private patrols
segments.body: A local group has discussed patrolling the area. Police strongly discourage private patrol groups, saying public safety and dealing with suspects are their responsibility, and that private patrols could have the opposite effect on people’s sense of security. Police are asking witnesses to contact them on 114.

content.headline: DTU investigates data breach that may affect 200,000 people
content.shortHeadline:
DTU breach may affect
up to 200,000 people
content.standfirst: The university says attackers accessed personal data dating back to 2003, but it does not yet know what information was taken or how many people are affected.

image.caption: DTU says an attack exposed its internal database to unauthorised access.

sources.originalTitle: DTU ramt af "alvorligt" hackerangreb – op mod 200.000 kan være berørt

segments.body: The Technical University of Denmark says an attacker accessed DTUBase, its internal system, and that up to 200,000 current and former users may be affected. The university says it has contained the breach and is working with external specialists to establish its scope.

segments.title: What data may be involved
segments.body: The accessed records reach back to 2003 and include names and CPR numbers, according to DTU. Some former users’ addresses, profile pictures and information about relatives are automatically deleted after six months. The university says it cannot yet confirm which records were taken or how many people are affected; the identity of the attackers is unknown.

segments.title: Advice for users
segments.body: DTU says it has reported the breach to the Danish Data Protection Agency and relevant authorities. It plans to contact current and former staff and almost all current and former students. The university advises people who may be affected to watch for suspicious calls, texts and emails, and to change passwords if they reused their DTU password elsewhere.

content.headline: G7 countries agree coordinated release of oil as fuel prices surge
content.shortHeadline:
G7 agrees oil release
as fuel prices rise
content.standfirst: A French G7 statement says a coordinated release will total 100 million barrels, including diesel. The timing and details of any European release remain in discussion.

image.caption: Trump is pressing for action to bring down fuel prices.

sources.originalTitle: G7-landene vil frigive 100 millioner tønder olie
Trump varsler forbud mod salg af olie – kan få "meget dramatiske konsekvenser"

segments.body: The G7 will release 100 million barrels of oil through a coordinated process with the International Energy Agency, according to the French G7 presidency. The four-month release is to begin immediately and include a substantial amount of diesel in its first 20 days.

segments.title: Pressure over diesel supplies
segments.body: US President Donald Trump said European countries had agreed to release large quantities of diesel “immediately” and had previously threatened to restrict US diesel exports unless allies released reserves. The EU has urged Washington to drop the threat, warning that a ban would undermine trust in the US as a reliable partner.

segments.title: Next steps remain unclear
segments.body: The EU’s member states were due to discuss a coordinated response to rising fuel prices and possible restrictions on US exports. Danish EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen said discussions were under way about when reserves might be released. The reporting does not specify how much Denmark will contribute or the exact timing of any national release.

content.headline: Danish military report leaves questions over suspected drones in Borris
content.shortHeadline:
Borris drone report
leaves questions open
content.standfirst: A revised account says soldiers did not fire at a plane, but cannot rule out commercial aircraft nearby. The identity of the suspected drone operators remains unknown.

image.caption: Army chief Peter Boysen presented the revised report on the Borris incident.

sources.originalTitle: Redaktør om dronesag: 'Det kan godt være, at de ikke skød mod et fly, men de skød i hvert fald sig selv i foden'
Hvordan kunne mystisk sort kassevogn forsvinde fra militær og politiet i den vestjyske efterårsnat?

segments.body: A revised Danish defence report says soldiers at Borris training area observed suspected drones and fired towards them in September 2025. The military says commercial aircraft may have been in the area, but that the aircraft were outside the projectiles’ range and were not fired upon.

segments.title: Questions about the response
segments.body: A defence editor quoted by DR said the revised account was more credible but criticised the military’s handling of the timeline and public communication. A defence academy lecturer also called the new details credible, while saying the earlier imprecision was not appropriate in a closely watched case.

segments.title: An unidentified vehicle
segments.body: The report describes a black van that drove away from the area after soldiers noticed it, but its role is unknown. An expert told DR that similar vehicles have been observed near drone incidents elsewhere, while stressing that he could not say whether that happened here. The report does not identify who operated the suspected drones or provide documentation confirming the observations.

content.headline: Copenhagen committee to decide future of Aarhus seaplane route
content.shortHeadline:
Copenhagen weighs future
of Aarhus seaplane
content.standfirst: The city administration recommends refusing a permanent environmental permit. The operator disputes its interpretation of the rules ahead of a 5 October committee decision.

image.caption: The seaplane route between Nordre Toldbod and Aarhus opened in 2016.

sources.originalTitle: Vandfly kan snart være fortid

segments.body: Copenhagen’s climate, environment and technology committee is due to decide on 5 October whether to reject a permanent environmental permit for Nordic Seaplanes at Nordre Toldbod. If the recommendation is followed, the company could lose permission when its current permit expires on 1 January 2027.

segments.title: Operator disputes the case
segments.body: The company’s director says the administration has misinterpreted the rules and points to a proposal to extend the floating pier by 12 metres to meet noise limits. He argues that actual noise reaching land is below the relevant limits. The municipality had not responded to TV 2 by publication.

segments.title: Opposing views on the harbour
segments.body: Some councillors support keeping the route, citing its potential contribution to electric seaplanes. Others say the harbour should prioritise public recreation and avoid noise and air pollution. The company says losing the permit could make it impossible to resume operations even if it later wins an appeal.

content.headline: Roskilde homeowners challenge order to remove unapproved coastal defences
content.shortHeadline:
Homeowners fight order
to remove coastal defences
content.standfirst: Eleven owners say their structures protect homes from flooding; the municipality says they were built without permission and obstruct public beach access.

image.caption: Roskilde Municipality says the structures restrict public passage along the coast.

sources.originalTitle: Jørgen og hans naboer trodser kommunen: Nægter at fjerne milliondyr kystsikring

segments.body: Eleven property owners by Roskilde Fjord say they will appeal an order to remove coastal protection structures they built without municipal permission. They say erosion and storm flooding threaten their homes. The owners say the work cost more than two million kroner.

segments.title: The municipality’s objection
segments.body: Roskilde Municipality says the structures are too close to the water and impede public passage along the coast. A municipal committee has ordered their removal, and the owners have also been reported to police. The owners argue they acted in good faith after years of dialogue with the municipality.

segments.title: Appeal ahead
segments.body: The owners have a year to remove the structures, but an appeal could extend the process. The committee chair says the municipality needs consistent rules for similar projects in the area and that the owners were told the work could not proceed as proposed.

content.headline: Person found dead after major fire in Nyborg row houses
content.shortHeadline:
Person found dead after
Nyborg row-house fire
content.standfirst: Police have not confirmed whether the deceased is a 70-year-old resident reported missing. They say there is no indication of a criminal act.

sources.originalTitle: Person fundet død efter brand i Nyborg
Mand savnet efter voldsom brand i rækkehuse

segments.body: A person has been found dead during police investigations into a fire that damaged several row houses at Møllerparken in Nyborg. Police have not yet identified the deceased and cannot confirm whether it is the 70-year-old resident reported missing after the fire.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The fire broke out on Thursday evening and was brought under control on Friday. Police are still investigating its cause and say there is currently no indication of a criminal act.

content.headline: Chinese car brands nearly double their Danish market share
content.shortHeadline:
Chinese car brands
gain ground in Denmark
content.standfirst: Chinese-owned marques reached a reported 12.3% of the Danish market this year, intensifying pressure on European manufacturers.

sources.originalTitle: Kinesiske biler får stort gennembrud i Danmark

segments.body: Chinese-owned car brands have increased their Danish market share from 7.5% in 2025 to 12.3% in 2026, according to TV 2. Brands including Xpeng, MG and Zeekr are driving the growth, with several recording sharp year-on-year rises.

segments.title: A challenge for European makers
segments.body: The report describes competition from lower-priced Chinese electric vehicles as a growing challenge for European manufacturers, especially Volkswagen Group. Industry analyst Ferdinand Dudenhoeffer points to Chinese manufacturers’ battery technology and faster development cycles, while also highlighting differences in labour costs.

segments.title: Trade and production
segments.body: The EU has imposed an average tariff of about 20% on Chinese imports, which it says receive state support.
